I am 68 years old and have farmed my land in Quzhou County for more than forty years. My six mu of flat, irrigated land sits on the North China Plain, and I know this soil well. At my age, I do not gamble with unfamiliar crops or risky new techniques—I stick with what has fed my family reliably: the winter wheat–summer maize double-cropping rotation that every experienced farmer in Hebei trusts.

My wheat is already in the ground, sown last October after the maize harvest. I use Jimai 22, an improved variety that performs steadily in our climate. Before sowing, I worked the field with rotary tillage to break up the maize stubble and create a fine seedbed. Now that spring has arrived, I will manage the wheat carefully: four irrigations—overwinter recovery, jointing, heading, and grain-filling—because water is the single biggest factor in reaching a good yield of around 1000 kg per mu. I apply nitrogen in split doses, totaling about 20 kg per mu, plus phosphate and potash to keep the soil balanced after decades of heavy cropping. I spray pesticides four times: a herbicide early, then fungicide and insecticide as the weather warms and diseases like rust or aphids appear.

Come early June, I will harvest the wheat and immediately plant Denghai 605 hybrid maize, the same variety most of my neighbors use because it tolerates our summer heat and gives strong yields. I will not till the soil again—no-tillage planting saves precious days between crops, preserves soil moisture, and reduces fuel costs. Maize needs less water than wheat here, so two irrigations are enough, one at the jointing stage and another at silking. I will top-dress with nitrogen and keep phosphorus and potassium moderate, about 18 kg N, 5 kg P₂O₅, and 5 kg K₂O per mu. Three rounds of pesticides protect the crop from corn borers and weeds.

I have some schooling, so I read the guidance from the agricultural extension office and adjust my fertilizer rates rather than copying what my father did exactly. But I am also practical: at 68, I hire machinery for harvesting and some spraying, and I keep my inputs conservative—no experimental crops, no over-investment. Wheat and maize give me roughly 1000 kg and 1150 kg per mu respectively, enough for household grain security and a modest cash income from the surplus. That is the plan, and I will follow it.
